About the author
Thiago Maior is the founder and CEO of EZOps Cloud, a DevOps and cloud infrastructure
consultancy specializing in scalable and automated cloud engineering for start-ups and
enterprise teams worldwide. With more than 20 years of experience in software engineering
and over a decade in DevOps and cloud operations, he has led hundreds of projects involving
CI/CD, distributed systems, and infrastructure automation. In 2016, he founded EZOps Cloud
to help organizations modernize and scale their cloud environments. In 2025, he launched ACE
Dev, the first agentic AI cloud engineer, advancing the use of artificial intelligence to automate
and accelerate cloud engineering workflows.
This book is the result of 10 years of work with over 200 people. What we built demanded countless
hours, late nights, weekends, and shared resilience. The entire EZOps Cloud team—engineers, staff,
and leadership—pushed this mission forward with discipline, grit, and vision. What began in Brazil
and now thrives in the US exists because of each of you.
About the reviewer
Thu Kha Kyawe is a Cloud and Site Reliability Engineer specializing in AWS infrastructure,
DevOps practices, and cloud automation. He has extensive hands-on experience architecting,
deploying, and operating scalable, production-grade cloud environments, with a strong
emphasis on infrastructure as code, CI/CD pipeline design, containerized workloads,
observability, and system reliability.
His work focuses on building secure, resilient, and highly available distributed systems that
support modern engineering teams. He holds AWS certifications and continually refines his
expertise through real-world implementations, architectural design, and operational
optimization initiatives. He has a strong interest in reliability engineering, automation
strategy, and designing cloud platforms that are scalable, maintainable, and performance-
driven.
Beyond his core engineering responsibilities, Thu Kha Kyawe actively contributes technical
insights and practical knowledge to the broader cloud and DevOps community.

Preface
The world of software delivery has undergone a seismic transformation over the past decade.
Where once it took weeks or months to ship a new feature to users, modern engineering teams
can now deploy dozens of changes to production every single day, with greater reliability and
less risk than ever before. This revolution has a name: DevOps. It is powered by a set of tools
and practices that were, until recently, the exclusive domain of large technology companies.
Not anymore.
This book is a practical, hands-on guide to the complete modern DevOps stack. It is designed
to take you from the foundational principles of DevOps culture and cloud computing all the
way through containerization, infrastructure as code, automated CI/CD pipelines, container
orchestration with Kubernetes, and beyond. You will not just read about these concepts, you
will build real systems, run real pipelines, and deploy real applications to the cloud. By the
time you reach the final chapter, you will have assembled a complete software factory, end to
end, using the same tools and workflows that power today's most innovative technology
organizations.
Whether you are a developer looking to take ownership of your deployments, a sysadmin
modernizing your skill set, or an ambitious professional building toward a cloud career, this
book will meet you where you are and take you further than you imagined. The journey begins
here.
Who this book is for
This book is written for software developers, system administrators, and IT professionals who
want to build practical, job-ready skills in DevOps and cloud engineering. If you have some
experience writing code or working with Linux systems and want to understand how modern
software is built, tested, secured, and deployed at scale, this book is for you. It is also an ideal
guide for career changers and freelancers who want to enter the high-demand field of cloud
and DevOps engineering. No prior experience with DevOps tools is required, but a basic
comfort with the command line and a willingness to get your hands dirty with real
infrastructure will help you get the most out of every chapter.

Understanding the DevOps and
Cloud Landscape
Welcome to the start of your journey into the worlds of DevOps and cloud computing. This
chapter lays the essential groundwork, introducing the core concepts that have revolutionized
how modern software is developed, delivered, and maintained. We will explore the cultural
and historical shifts that led to DevOps and demystify the fundamental services that form the
backbone of the cloud. You will move from theory to the first steps of practice, understanding
how these two domains merge to create efficient, automated, and scalable software delivery
pipelines. By the end of this chapter, you will not only grasp what DevOps and the cloud are
but also why they are indispensable in today's technology landscape. You'll have a clear map of
the principles and players involved, preparing you for the hands-on tasks in the chapters to
come.
In this chapter, we're going to cover the following main topics:
What is DevOps? A new culture of collaboration
From Agile to DevOps: A brief history
The DevOps lifecycle: From code to operation
Core principles: Automation, continuous integration, and continuous delivery
Introduction to cloud computing: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
Major cloud players: AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud

Technical requirements
For this chapter, the primary requirements are a willingness to learn and a web browser to
explore some of the concepts discussed. As we are focusing on foundational knowledge, there
are no specific software installations needed yet. You will be guided on creating accounts with
major cloud providers later in the book.
What is DevOps? A new culture of collaboration
In this section, we will explore the idx_223fe83c fundamental concept of DevOps. We'll begin by defining
what it is, and what it isn't, and discuss why it is best understood as a cultural shift rather than
just a set of tools or a specific job title. The primary goal is to understand how DevOps fosters
collaboration between traditionally "separated" teams, particularly Development (Dev) and
Operations (Ops), to deliver better software faster. This understanding is the bedrock upon
which all other technical skills in this book are built.
Deconstructing the "wall of confusion"
At its heart, DevOps represents a profound change in mindset. To truly appreciate this shift, we
must first travel back in time to a typical software company before DevOps became
mainstream. In this era, the idx_4ddb4665 organizational structure created a natural and often adversarial
divide between the people who built the software and the people who operated the software.
These two groups, Development and Operations, worked in separate silos, each with its own
goals, incentives, and vocabulary.

The Development team's primary mission was to create new features. They were measured on
their ability to innovate and deliver functionality requested by the business. Their world was
one of constant change, driven by deadlines and the pressure to release the "next big thing."
Once they finished writing and testing their code in a controlled development environment,
their job was largely considered done. The finished product was then handed over to the
Operations team.

The Operations team, on the other hand, had a completely different mandate: to ensure the
stability, reliability, and performance of the production environment. Their world was one of
stability and risk mitigation. They were measured on uptime, system health, and their ability
to prevent outages. From their perspective, every new release from the Development team was
a potential source of instability, a threat to the very metrics they were judged by.
This fundamental conflict of interest created what the DevOps community famously calls the
"wall of confusion." It was a metaphorical, yet very real, barrier that hindered communication,
collaboration, and trust. Developers would "throw code over the wall" to Operations, often
with minimal documentation or consideration for how it would behave in a live environment.
The Operations team would then be left to deploy and manage this unfamiliar code, often
discovering issues with configuration, dependencies, or performance only after it was live and
affecting real users.
When problems inevitably occurred, the blame game would begin. Operations would accuse
Development of delivering buggy, unstable code. Development would retort that the code
worked perfectly on their machines and that Operations must have configured the
environment incorrectly.
This cycle of conflict led to several negative outcomes:
Slow release cycles: Fear of production failures led to long, bureaucratic release
processes with extensive idx_fac05b5e manual checks, delaying the delivery of value to customers
Low-quality releases: Without collaboration, developers lacked insight into
production realities, and operations lacked input into the development process,
resulting in software that was not designed for operational excellence
High failure rates: The disconnect between teams meant that many issues were only
caught in production, leading to frequent outages and emergency "firefighting"
Poor morale: The constant friction and finger-pointing created a toxic work
environment characterized by stress, burnout, and a lack of mutual respect
DevOps was born out of the necessity to dismantle this wall. It proposes a radical idea: what if
Development and Operations weren't adversaries, but partners on the same team with a
single, shared objective? That objective is the fast, efficient, and reliable delivery of value to the
customer.
The three pillars of DevOps culture
DevOps is not a tool you idx_d341d6fa can buy or a process you can simply install. It is a cultural philosophy
that must be adopted and nurtured. This culture rests on three foundational pillars that guide
the interactions between teams and individuals.
•
•
•

5 Understanding the DevOps and Cloud Landscape
1. Shared ownership and systems thinking
The first pillar is a shift from siloed responsibility to collective ownership. In a DevOps culture,

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 4
chunks.content:
the idx_a7b639b4 entire team, including developers, operations engineers, QA testers, security analysts, and
product managers, shares responsibility for the software's success throughout its entire
lifecycle. This concept is often summarized by the phrase, "You build it, you run it."
This means a developer's job doesn't end when they commit their code. They are also
responsible for ensuring that their code can be deployed, monitored, and supported in
production. This encourages them to think about operational concerns from the very
beginning. They might ask questions such as the following:
How will we monitor the health of this new service?
How can we configure this application without manual intervention?
Is this feature designed to be scalable and resilient?
Conversely, the Operations team's role shifts from being a gatekeeper to an enabler. Instead of
manually deploying applications, they focus on building automated platforms and self-service
tools that empower developers to deploy and manage their own services safely and efficiently.
They become consultants and collaborators, offering their expertise on infrastructure, security,
and scalability early in the design process.
This pillar is rooted in systems thinking, the ability to see the entire software delivery process
as a single, integrated system, rather than a collection of disconnected parts. The goal is to
idx_ce8bfd32 optimize the overall flow of value from idea to end user, not just to optimize individual tasks
within a silo. When everyone shares ownership of the entire system, decisions are made for the
greater good of the product, not just for the convenience of one team.
2. Faster and amplified feedback loops
The second pillar is the conscious cultivation of empathy and the creation of fast, continuous
feedback idx_11e2d1cc loops. Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of another. In a
DevOps context, it means developers understanding the pressures of maintaining a 24/7
production environment, and operations engineers understanding the business need for rapid
innovation.
When a developer is woken up at 3 A.M. by an alert caused by their own code, they develop a
profound empathy for the on-call operations engineer. This experience naturally incentivizes
them to write more robust, resilient, and observable code in the future. Practices such as
having developers participate in on-call rotations are a direct application of this principle.
Empathy is fostered by amplifying feedback loops. The "wall of confusion" created long, slow
feedback loops. A bug discovered in production might take weeks to be reported back to the
•
•

developer who introduced it, by which time they would have moved on to other tasks. DevOps
seeks to shorten these loops, providing feedback as quickly and as early as possible.
Examples of idx_1af61f3d amplified feedback loops include the following:
Continuous integration: Developers get immediate feedback on whether their code
changes integrate correctly with the rest of the code base
Automated testing: Automated tests provide instant feedback on the quality and
correctness of the code
Monitoring and observability: Real-time monitoring of the production environment
idx_2d7ac3e8 provides immediate feedback on the performance and health of the application
Direct customer feedback: Channels are created to get feedback directly from users
back to the development team
By creating idx_1bf3bbe7 these fast feedback loops, teams can detect and correct problems when they are
small, cheap, and easy to fix, rather than waiting for them to become large, expensive, and
catastrophic failures in production.
3. A culture of continuous improvement and experimentation
The third idx_399abf85 pillar is a relentless focus on continuous improvement and a willingness to
experiment. This principle acknowledges that there is no such thing as a perfect process or a
finished system. There are always opportunities to improve, to remove waste, and to become
more efficient.
This requires creating a high-trust environment where it is safe to fail. If every failure is met
with blame and punishment, people will be afraid to try new things, and innovation will
stagnate. In a healthy DevOps culture, failures are treated as learning opportunities. When an
incident occurs, the focus is not on finding someone to blame, but on understanding the
systemic causes of the failure. This is often accomplished through a blameless post-mortem
process, where the team collaboratively deconstructs the incident to identify weaknesses in the
system and process, and then defines concrete actions to prevent similar failures in the future.
This culture encourages experimentation. Teams are empowered to try new tools, refactor old
code, and challenge existing processes in the pursuit of improvement. This might involve the
following:
A/B testing: Experimenting with different versions of a feature to see which one
performs better with users
Kaizen events: Dedicated time set aside for teams to focus on process improvement
Learning days: Encouraging team members to spend time learning new skills and
technologies

7 Understanding the DevOps and Cloud Landscape
By fostering a culture of continuous learning and experimentation, organizations can adapt
and evolve in the face of changing technology and business requirements. They avoid the
stagnation that comes from believing "this is the way we've always done it."

chunks.content:
By embracing these three pillars, shared ownership, amplified feedback, and continuous
improvement, organizations can successfully break down the "wall of confusion" and build a
thriving DevOps culture. This cultural foundation is the essential prerequisite for successfully
implementing the technical practices and tools that we will explore throughout the rest of this
book.
With idx_55dc0f76 these cultural foundations in place, it's helpful to step back and understand how DevOps
itself emerged. By tracing its roots in Agile and related movements, we can see why these
pillars became necessary and how they continue to shape modern software delivery.
From Agile to DevOps: A brief history
DevOps did not appear in a idx_f9edaa28 vacuum. It is the logical and evolutionary next step in a decades-
long journey to find better ways of building and delivering software. To understand why
DevOps emerged and why it is so powerful, we must first look at its direct predecessor: the
Agile movement. This section traces the path from the rigid, sequential models of the idx_252aef88 past to
the flexible, collaborative frameworks that set the stage for the DevOps revolution.
The age of Waterfall: A linear approach
Before Agile, the dominant methodology for idx_efdd434d software development was the Waterfall model.
As its name idx_73a59201 suggests, this model was a linear, sequential process where each phase of
development had to be fully completed before the next one could begin. A typical Waterfall
project flowed downwards through a series of distinct stages:
Requirements: The project would begin with a lengthy phase of gathering and
documenting every conceivable requirement for the system. This often resulted in a
massive, multi-hundred-page document that was "signed off" by the stakeholders.
Design: Based on the requirements document, architects and senior developers would
create a complete design for the entire system, specifying the architecture, data models,
and interfaces.
Implementation: With the design complete, programmers would begin the long
process of writing the code for the entire system.
Testing: Once all the code idx_2c6c6f28 was written, the Quality Assurance (QA) team would begin
a dedicated testing phase to find and report bugs.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 8
chunks.content:
Chapter 1 8
Deployment: After the software was deemed stable enough, the Operations team
would deploy it to the production environment.
Maintenance: The project would then enter a long-term maintenance phase, where
any bugs or requests for minor changes were handled.
The Waterfall model was borrowed from manufacturing and construction industries, where
making changes late in the process is prohibitively expensive. You cannot easily add a new
floor to a idx_43f85fe1 skyscraper after the roof is on. The assumption was that software development could
be just as predictable. However, this assumption proved to be deeply flawed.
The cracks in the Waterfall
While logical on paper, the Waterfall idx_5903f0cf model consistently failed to deliver successful software
projects. The core problem was its inflexibility in the face of change. Software is not a physical
building; its requirements are fluid and often poorly understood at the outset. The Waterfall
model suffered from several critical weaknesses:
Late feedback: Customers and users would not see any working software until the very
end of the project, often months or even years after it began. By then, their needs had
often changed, and the delivered product no longer solved their problem.
High risk: The model concentrated all the risk at the end of the project. A fundamental
flaw in the initial requirements or design might not be discovered until the testing
phase, at which point it is incredibly expensive and time-consuming to fix.
Lack of adaptability: The model assumed that all requirements could be known
upfront. This is rarely the case. The business world changes, new technologies emerge,
and a better understanding of the problem develops over time. Waterfall had no
mechanism to gracefully incorporate these changes.
The software industry was in a state of crisis. Projects were consistently late, over budget, and
failed to meet user expectations. It was clear that a new approach was needed, one that
embraced change rather than resisting it.
The Agile revolution: Embracing change
In the 1990s, a group of software developers began experimenting with new, lightweight
development processes that stood in stark contrast to the heavyweight, documentation-driven
Waterfall model. These new idx_0760e51d methods focused on iterative development, close customer
collaboration, and delivering working software in small, frequent increments.
In 2001, seventeen of these software pioneers met at a ski resort in Utah to discuss their shared
ideas. The result of this meeting was the Manifesto for Agile Software Development, a

document that would change the course of the software industry. The Agile Manifesto is
defined by four core values:
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Responding to change over following a plan
The manifesto idx_3faf8535 clarifies that while there is value in the items on the right, the items on the left
are valued more. This was a radical departure from the Waterfall mindset. Agile was not a
single, prescriptive methodology, but rather a set of guiding principles. From these principles,
several popular frameworks emerged, most notably Scrum and Kanban.
Scrum: Iterating in Sprints
Scrum is an Agile framework that structures idx_dbd499a7 development in short, time-boxed iterations
called Sprints. A Sprint idx_19b35209 is typically one to four weeks long, and its goal is to produce a
potentially shippable increment idx_52bef2db of working software.
The Scrum framework is defined by a set of roles, events, and artifacts:
Roles:
The Product Owner is responsible for idx_126e31de defining the features of the idx_7d745860 product and
prioritizing the work
The Development Team is a idx_65e1d9e0 self-organizing group of individuals who do the
work of building the software
The Scrum Master is a idx_f3db1283 servant-leader who helps the team follow the Scrum
process and removes any impediments to their progress
Events: Each Sprint contains a idx_965f9805 series of meetings or events.
Sprint Planning happens idx_c9c888a4 at the beginning of the Sprint, where the team
decides what work can be accomplished
Daily Scrum (or stand-up) is a idx_f5349ef6 short, 15-minute meeting each day for the team
to coordinate their work

Scrum introduced a rhythm of iterative development and continuous feedback that allowed
teams to adapt to changing requirements and deliver value to customers much more quickly
than the Waterfall model.
Kanban: Visualizing the flow of work
Kanban is another popular idx_61b9e7fc Agile framework that originated in the manufacturing world,
specifically from the Toyota Production System. Unlike the time-boxed Sprints of Scrum,
Kanban is a flow-based system. The core idea is to visualize the workflow, limit the amount of
work in progress (WIP), and optimize idx_8fb0299f the flow of work from start to finish.
A Kanban system is typically implemented using a Kanban board, which has a series of
columns representing the stages of the workflow (e.g., To Do, In Progress, In Test, Done). Work
items, represented by cards, move from left to right across the board as they are completed. By
setting explicit limits on how many items can be in any given column at one time (WIP limits),
the team can prevent bottlenecks and ensure a smooth, continuous flow of work. Kanban is
particularly useful for teams that deal with a high volume of unplanned work, such as support
or operations teams.
The last mile problem: Where Agile ended
The Agile movement was a phenomenal success. It dramatically improved the way software
was written, breaking down the barriers between developers and business stakeholders (such
as product managers and idx_1f1e9e26 customers). Teams were now able to produce high-quality, working
software in small, frequent batches. However, a new bottleneck emerged.
While the development process had become fast and iterative, the deployment process was
often still slow, manual, and painful, a remnant of the old Waterfall world. The Agile Manifesto
focused primarily on the process of developing software. It was largely silent on the topic of
delivering and operating that software.
This created a new version of the "wall of confusion." The Development team, now highly
Agile, was producing new features at a rapid pace. They would finish a Sprint and have a new

increment of software ready to go. But the Operations team, which was not part of the Agile

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 10
chunks.content:
transformation, was still operating with the old mindset of minimizing change and risk. They
could not keep up with the pace of the Agile developers. This friction between a fast-moving
"Dev" and a slow-moving "Ops" became known as the "last mile problem."
It was in this context that DevOps was born. In 2009, at an O'Reilly Velocity conference, two
engineers named John Allspaw and Paul Hammond gave a groundbreaking presentation titled
10+ Deploys Per Day: Dev and Ops Cooperation at Flickr. They described how their Development
and Operations teams worked together as a single, integrated unit, using automation and
shared tools to deploy software to production multiple times a day with confidence.
This talk inspired a Belgian consultant named Patrick Debois, who was frustrated by the very
same Dev versus Ops conflict. He coined the term "DevOps" and organized the first
"DevOpsDays" conference in idx_1b20bb89 Ghent, Belgium. The movement had a name, and it began to
spread rapidly.
DevOps is not a replacement for Agile; it is an extension of it. It takes the principles of
collaboration, small batches, and fast feedback from Agile and extends them beyond the code
commit, all the way through to production deployment and operation. It is the solution to the
"last mile problem," completing the journey that Agile started by bringing Development and
Operations together to create a seamless, end-to-end system for delivering value.
Now that we understand the cultural and historical context of DevOps, let's examine the
practical application of its principles in the following section.
The DevOps lifecycle: From code to operation
The DevOps lifecycle is not a linear process like Waterfall, but rather a continuous and iterative
loop. It represents the seamless flow of work from the initial idea all the way to the end user,
and the subsequent feedback idx_c4893623 that flows back to inspire the next idea. This lifecycle is often
visualized as an infinite loop, symbolizing the ongoing nature of software development and
improvement.
While different diagrams may use slightly different terms, the lifecycle can generally be broken
down into eight key phases. These phases are not strictly sequential; they often overlap, and
teams may be working in multiple phases simultaneously. The goal is to make the journey
through this loop as fast, efficient, and reliable as possible through a combination of
collaboration, automation, and feedback. This is often represented as the DevOps infinity loop:

Figure 1.1: The DevOps infinity loop
The diagram highlights the eight interconnected stages: Plan, Code, Build, Test, Release,
Deploy, Operate, and Monitor. We idx_5fc0449e will be exploring them in the following subsections.
Phase 1: Plan
Every journey begins with a plan. In the DevOps lifecycle, the planning phase is where the
vision for the software is defined, and idx_74a2a928 the work is organized. This is a highly collaborative
phase that involves input from all stakeholders, including product managers, developers,
operations engineers, and even customers. The goal is to define what needs to be built, why it
needs to be built, and how it will be delivered.
Unlike the rigid requirements-gathering phase of the Waterfall model, DevOps planning is
agile and adaptive. The work is broken down into small, manageable pieces, often called user
stories or features. These work items are captured and prioritized in a backlog. This phase is
less about creating a perfect, long-term plan and more about defining the immediate next
steps and ensuring that everyone on the team has a clear and shared understanding of the
goals.
The following are the key activities in this stage:
Defining business value and success metrics
Creating and prioritizing user stories in a product backlog
Estimating the effort required for work items
Planning the work for the next iteration or sprint

Planning activities are facilitated by project and work management tools. Agile project
management idx_5e5a7499 and issue tracking are handled by Jira, Azure Boards, and Pivotal Tracker, while
Trello provides lightweight task and workflow management for teams preferring visual boards.
Phase 2: Code
Once the plan is in place, the development work begins. In the code phase, developers take the
work items from the backlog and translate them into software. This is where the core logic and
functionality of the application are idx_96a65b6b created. However, in a DevOps culture, coding is about
more than just writing functional code. It also involves writing code that is clean,
maintainable, and testable.
A critical practice in this phase is version control. All idx_9429fcfd code and related artifacts (such as
configuration files) are stored in a shared code repository. This allows multiple developers to
work on the same code base simultaneously, track changes over time, and collaborate
effectively. The dominant version control system used today is Git.
The following are the key activities in this stage:
Writing application code
Writing unit tests to verify the code's correctness
Peer code reviews to ensure quality and share knowledge
Committing code to a shared version control repository
The common tools used to do these things can be categorized by function. Git serves as the

version control system, while platforms such as GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket provide code
hosting and idx_46c24584 collaboration capabilities. Development work is typically done in Integrated
Development Environments (IDEs) such as VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA.
Phase 3: Build
The build phase is where the source code is compiled and packaged into a runnable
application. This is one of the idx_9b8c089a first major steps in automation. Instead of developers manually
building the application on their own machines, a dedicated, automated system takes idx_7e9ade8b over.
This system is known as a Continuous Integration (CI) server.
When a developer commits new code to the repository, it triggers an automated build process.
The CI server pulls the latest version of the code, compiles it, and runs any associated unit
tests. If the build or the tests fail, the CI server immediately notifies the team. This provides a
rapid feedback loop, allowing developers to quickly identify and fix integration issues. The
output of a successful build is an artifact, a packaged, versioned, and deployable unit of the
software (e.g., a JAR file, a Docker image, or a ZIP archive).

The following are the key activities in this stage:
Compiling source code
Running unit and integration tests
Packaging the application into a deployable artifact
Storing the artifact in a repository
The common tools used to implement these activities are: For CI/CD orchestration and
automation, teams typically use Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, CircleCI,
or AWS CodePipeline. Build and dependency management is handled by tools such as Maven
and idx_185aec83 Gradle, while Docker provides containerization capabilities. Artifact repositories such as
Docker Hub, JFrog Artifactory, and Nexus Repository store build outputs, and unit testing is
performed using frameworks such as Google Test, JUnit, and pytest.
Phase 4: Test
While some testing happens during the build phase (unit tests), the test phase involves more
comprehensive and rigorous quality assurance. The goal is to ensure that the new version of
the software not only works as idx_80dd7b5c expected but also doesn't introduce any regressions (i.e., break
existing functionality). This phase is heavily automated to provide fast and reliable feedback
on the quality of the release candidate.
Automated tests can include a wide variety of types:
Integration tests: Verifying that different idx_07223a0f parts of the application work together
correctly
End-to-end tests: Simulating user idx_2b730c16 journeys through the entire application
Performance tests: Checking idx_f42568d1 the application's speed, scalability, and stability under
load
Security tests: Scanning the application idx_801c5954 for known vulnerabilities
The deployable artifact from the build phase is deployed to a dedicated testing environment,
and the automated test suites are run against it. If all tests pass, the team gains confidence that
the artifact is ready for release.
The following are the key activities in this stage:
Deploying the application to a test environment
Executing automated test suites
Analyzing test results and reporting defects
Performing manual exploratory testing where needed

Testing activities rely on specialized tools for different purposes. Automated UI and end-to-
end testing idx_49cc6993 are performed using Selenium and Cypress, while JMeter handles performance and
load testing. API testing is typically done with Postman, code quality and static analysis with
SonarQube, and security vulnerability scanning with Snyk.
Phase 5: Release
Once an artifact has successfully passed all the automated tests, it is considered a release
candidate. The release phase is the idx_d142dd70 final checkpoint before deployment to production. This
phase involves preparing the artifact for release and obtaining any necessary final approvals.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide

chunks.content:
In a mature DevOps organization, this phase is often fully automated. The process of
promoting a build from testing to a release candidate is handled by the automation server. This
is the core of Continuous Delivery (CD). The system ensures that every change that passes the
automated tests results in a production-ready idx_81c96d8c artifact. However, the decision to actually push
that artifact to production is still a manual one, based on business needs. This allows the
organization to release on demand, rather than being tied to a rigid schedule.
It's worth noting that CD can also stand for Continuous Deployment, which takes automation
one step further. While Continuous Delivery automates the pipeline up to the production
deployment but requires manual approval for the final release, Continuous Deployment fully
automates the entire process, including the deployment to production. In Continuous
Deployment, every change that passes all automated tests is automatically released to
production without human intervention.
The following are the key activities in this stage:
Tagging and versioning the release candidate
Generating release notes
Obtaining final business or manual approvals for deployment
Staging the release for production
Release management is supported by tools serving distinct functions. CI/CD orchestration and
release automation are handled by Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions, and Azure Pipelines.
Artifact repository management is performed using JFrog Artifactory and Nexus Repository,
while semantic-release automates semantic versioning and release naming based on commit
conventions.
Phase 6: Deploy
The deploy phase is where the new version of the software is pushed out to the production
environment and made available to end users. Like the build and test phases, this process
should be fully automated to make it fast, reliable, and repeatable. Manual deployments are
slow, error-prone, and a major source of production outages.

Chapter 1 16
Modern deployment automation idx_1a9655ce often involves the concept of Infrastructure as Code (IaC),
where the production environment itself is defined and managed through code. This idx_667fcc62 ensures
that the environment is consistent and reproducible. Deployment automation tools handle the
process of safely rolling out the new version of the application, often using advanced strategies
such as blue-green deployments or canary releases to minimize risk and downtime.
The following are the key activities in this stage:
Provisioning and configuring the production infrastructure
Automating the rollout of the new application version
Performing post-deployment health checks
Automating the rollback process in case of failure
Deployment is enabled through tools designed for specific infrastructure and orchestration
needs. IaC can be implemented using Terraform, OpenTofu or Pulumi. Container orchestration
is handled by Kubernetes and Docker Swarm, while ArgoCD provides GitOps-based
continuous deployment capabilities. Cloud-native deployment services include AWS
CodeDeploy and Azure DevOps.
Phase 7: Operate
The lifecycle doesn't end once the software is deployed. The Operate phase encompasses all the
activities required to manage idx_8d876ce0 the application in the production environment. This was
traditionally the exclusive domain of the Operations team, but in a DevOps culture, it is a
shared responsibility.
This phase includes tasks such as managing the underlying infrastructure, ensuring high
availability and fault tolerance, and implementing disaster recovery plans. The goal is to keep
the application running smoothly, securely, and efficiently. Much of this work is also
automated, using tools for auto-scaling, self-healing, and configuration management to
maintain the desired state of the system.
The following are the key activities in this stage:
Managing cloud infrastructure
Implementing high-availability and disaster-recovery solutions
Managing security and access control
Optimizing costs and performance
The common tools used to do these things are AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud.

Phase 8: Monitor
The final phase of the loop involves monitoring. This is where the feedback part of the loop
becomes most prominent. In this phase, the team continuously collects and analyzes data from
the production environment to idx_4c39e36b understand how the application is behaving and idx_7d97e813 how it is
being used. This practice is often referred to as observability.
Monitoring involves collecting three main types of data:
Logs: Detailed, time-stamped idx_3e6f0a56 records of events that occurred within the application or
system
Metrics: Numerical measurements idx_321b47a4 of the system's health and performance over time

chunks.content:
(e.g., CPU utilization, response time, error rate)
Traces: A detailed record of idx_bef37066 the journey of a single request as it travels through all the
different services in a distributed system
This data is fed into monitoring tools that provide dashboards, visualizations, and automated
alerts. The insights gained from monitoring are crucial. They help the team detect and
diagnose problems, understand the impact of new features, and make data-driven decisions
about future development. This data feeds directly back into the planning phase, closing the
loop and starting the next cycle of improvement.
The following are the key activities in this stage:
Collecting logs, metrics, and traces from the application and infrastructure
Creating dashboards to visualize system health
Setting up automated alerts for critical issues
Analyzing performance and usage data
The common tools used to do these things are Prometheus, Grafana, ELK Stack (Elasticsearch,
Logstash, Kibana), Datadog, New Relic, and Splunk.
By understanding and optimizing this continuous lifecycle, DevOps teams can create a
powerful engine for delivering high-quality software at high velocity. Each phase is an
opportunity for collaboration and automation, and the feedback loops between them ensure
that the team is always learning and improving.
If the DevOps lifecycle describes what happens, the core principles of DevOps describe how it
happens effectively. Let's look at that next.

Chapter 1 18
Core principles: Automation, continuous integration,
and continuous delivery
While the cultural pillars provide the mindset, the core principles are the technical engines
that drive the speed, quality, and reliability of the software delivery process. They are not just
best practices; they are foundational concepts that enable the entire DevOps paradigm to
function. In this section, we will delve into three of the most critical technical principles:
automation, continuous integration, and the closely related concepts of continuous
delivery and continuous deployment.
Automation: The engine of DevOps
At its core, DevOps is about flow and feedback. The single greatest inhibitor to both is manual,
repetitive work. Every manual idx_42e12fef task is a potential source of delay, human error, and
inconsistency. Automation is idx_908ab940 the practice of using technology to perform these tasks without
human intervention. In DevOps, the guiding philosophy is simple: automate everything that is
repeatable. This includes building, testing, analyzing, deploying, and even managing
infrastructure.
The benefits of aggressive automation are profound:
Speed: Automated processes run orders of magnitude faster than manual ones. A
deployment that might take idx_8c5628f2 a human hours of careful, step-by-step work can be
executed by an automated script in minutes. This dramatically shortens the lead time
from code commit to production release.
Reliability and consistency: Humans make mistakes, especially when performing
repetitive tasks. An automated process executes the exact same steps, in the exact same
way, every single time. This eliminates a huge class of errors caused by typos, missed
steps, or environmental differences.
Repeatability: Automation ensures that processes are repeatable. You can run the same
automated test suite or deployment script a thousand times and get the same result,
which is crucial for building confidence in your release process.
Empowerment: By automating tedious, low-value tasks, you free up your highly
skilled engineers to focus on high-value work, such as designing better systems,
innovating on new features, and improving processes. It replaces toil with engineering.
•
•
•
•
19 Understanding the DevOps and Cloud Landscape
A key practice that embodies the principle of automation is Infrastructure as Code (IaC),
which we will explore in detail in Chapter 5. With IaC, the entire infrastructure – servers,
networks, databases, and load balancers – is defined and managed using code, just like the
application itself. This allows you to create, update, and destroy entire environments in a fully
automated, repeatable, and version-controlled manner.
Continuous integration: The foundation of quality
Continuous Integration (CI) is a development idx_0e6edfc4 practice that directly addresses the problems

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 18
chunks.content:
of integrating code from multiple developers. In the pre-CI world, developers would often
work in isolation on their own features for weeks or even months. When it was finally time to
merge all these different streams of work into the main code base, the result was often a
painful and chaotic process known as "merge hell," where idx_15e82d8c countless conflicts and bugs would
surface, leading to long delays.
CI solves this problem by idx_aecc5341 requiring developers to integrate their work frequently, at least once
a day, and often multiple times a day. Each integration is then verified by an automated build-
and-test sequence. This practice is implemented using a CI server (such as Jenkins or GitHub
Actions) that monitors the central code repository.
The CI process typically follows these steps:
A developer commits a change to their local copy of the code.
The developer pushes the commit to the central version control repository (e.g., on
GitHub).
The CI server detects the new commit and triggers a new build job.
The CI server pulls the latest code, including the new change.
It compiles the code and packages it into a build artifact.
It runs a suite of automated tests (typically fast-running unit and integration tests)
against the artifact.
The CI server provides immediate feedback to the developer. If the build or any test
fails, the "build is broken," and the team is notified. The priority then becomes fixing
the build before any new work is done.
By integrating in small, frequent batches, teams can detect integration issues at the earliest
possible moment, when they are small and easy to fix. CI doesn't just automate the build; it
creates a powerful, rapid feedback loop that dramatically improves code quality and developer
productivity. It is the foundational practice upon which all other DevOps automation is built.

Chapter 1 20
Continuous delivery and continuous deployment: The path
to production
Once you have a reliable CI process that produces a high-quality build artifact with every code
change, the next logical step is to automate the rest of the release process. This is where
continuous delivery and continuous deployment come in. While the terms are often used
interchangeably, they represent two different levels of automation.
Continuous delivery
Continuous Delivery (CD) is the idx_6969d832 practice of extending CI to ensure that every change that
passes the automated tests is automatically idx_f10e013b prepared and staged for release to production. In a
continuous delivery pipeline, the artifact from the CI build flows through a series of
progressively more rigorous testing and staging environments. This might include
performance testing, security scanning, and user acceptance testing (UAT).
If the artifact successfully passes idx_70419c47 through all these stages, it is automatically deployed to a
staging environment and is considered "production-ready." The key aspect of CD is that the
final step, deploying to the actual production environment, is still a manual, business decision.
A product manager or team lead can decide when to release by simply clicking a button.
CD gives the business the capability to release new features, bug fixes, or experiments to users
safely and quickly at any time. It decouples the act of deployment from the act of release,
providing maximum flexibility.
Continuous deployment
Continuous Deployment (also CD) takes this one step further. It is the practice of
automatically deploying every change that idx_bd2061bf passes the entire automated pipeline directly to
production, without any human intervention. If a developer's idx_beabc15e change successfully makes it
through all the CI and CD stages, it will be live in front of users within minutes.
This is the pinnacle of release automation and requires a very high degree of confidence in your
automated testing and monitoring capabilities. Teams practicing CD often rely on advanced
deployment techniques such as canary releases (releasing the change to a small subset of users
first) and robust monitoring to quickly detect and roll back any issues. Companies such as
Amazon, Netflix, and Google practice CD, enabling them to release changes hundreds or even
thousands of times per day.
Together, CI and CD create a fully idx_54307ef0 automated deployment pipeline, a powerful, automated
pathway that takes code from a developer's workstation to the production environment. This
pipeline is the backbone of any high-performing DevOps organization, enabling the fast,
reliable, and low-risk delivery of software.
